title: From an alert to the right person
description: Separate alert matching, Watchlist inboxes and external delivery, and test the complete notification path.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Our fictional warehouse team wants to hear about activity at the entrance after closing. Is adding an email channel enough to make that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A channel is a destination, not the decision. An alert evaluates configured conditions, then a matching event can create a notification for recipients and send it through selected channels. Think about what matters and who needs to know.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So an inbox entry and an external message are related, but not identical?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Right. A notification can appear in Hub even if an external channel fails. Separating those steps makes troubleshooting much clearer: first check matching and recipients, then check delivery.

chapters.title: Use the Watchlist as an inbox

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The operator comes in the next morning. Where do they review what arrived?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The Watchlist is the signed-in recipient's inbox. It shows recent notifications, with filters and read state to help review them. Expanding an entry can reveal its details and the linked recording when media is available.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: If the event needs follow-up, can it become more than an unread item?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: When case creation is enabled, the operator can start a case from the notification. That's useful when the footage needs investigation and preservation rather than just a read marker in an inbox.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should the administrator check for our entrance-after-closing scenario?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Choose the intended devices, the active time range, and conditions supported by the deployment. If a classification is involved, its value must match the configured model's output. Then select the intended recipients or channels.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: No point in announcing warehouse activity to an empty room.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Exactly. Test one clear rule end to end. Managing alerts needs the appropriate administrative permission, so being able to read a notification doesn't mean being able to change the organisation's rules.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when the team updates its webhook or mail credentials?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Test the channel again. Confirm the destination accepts the request and reports success, and keep provider secrets in protected configuration. A visible Watchlist item can't prove an external service received the message.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And keeping the notification doesn't archive the footage forever?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Correct. Notifications remain subject to retention, and the Watchlist isn't an evidence archive. Create a case when the recording must outlast the ordinary window, and confirm the archive operation succeeds.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
